exam: A 58‑year‑old farmer with chronic cough presents with barrel chest; what is the next bedside maneuver to confirm hyperinflation? — Measure chest expansion and assess for pursed‑lip breathing.
Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.62 and TLC 140 % predicted; how does this differentiate COPD from restrictive disease? — Low ratio with high TLC indicates obstructive air‑trapping, not restriction.
A patient with known COPD develops sudden pleuritic chest pain; what complication must you rule out and how? — Suspect pneumothorax; obtain urgent chest X‑ray.
Why are inhaled anticholinergics preferred as first‑line in COPD with increased TLC? — They reduce bronchoconstriction without tachycardia, improving air‑trapping.
In a low‑resource clinic without spirometry, what clinical sign most strongly suggests increased TLC? — Barrel‑shaped chest with increased anterior‑posterior diameter.

A young adult with HIV presents with chronic cough and hyperinflated lungs on X‑ray; what infection should be considered and what test ordered? — Post‑TB bronchiectasis; order sputum microscopy for acid‑fast bacilli.
What vaccination strategy reduces future exacerbations in patients with increased TLC due to COPD? — Annual influenza and one‑time pneumococcal vaccination.

During follow‑up, a patient’s TLC rises from 130 % to 170 % predicted; what does this indicate and what action is needed? — Progression to moderate hyperinflation; intensify bronchodilator regimen and assess for exacerbation triggers.
ai.title: Increased Total Lung Capacity
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Increased total lung capacity (TLC) reflects expansion of lung volumes, often due to obstructive or restrictive lung disease, hyperinflation, or compensatory mechanisms. Recognising patterns of TLC, functional residual capacity and residual volume guides diagnosis in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Total lung capacity is the maximal volume of air in the lungs after a maximal inspiratory effort. An increased TLC is identified when spirometry or body plethysmography shows values >120 % predicted, together with raised functional residual capacity (FRC) and residual volume (RV).

t.b: Confirms increased TLC and distinguishes obstructive vs restrictive patterns; a high TLC with low FEV1/FVC suggests obstruction.
Shows hyperlucent lungs, flattened diaphragms, or barrel chest when plethysmography unavailable.
Provides bedside clue when equipment is lacking; excessive expansion suggests hyperinflation.

Patients often present with dyspnoea on exertion, a barrel‑shaped chest, and a prolonged expiratory phase. Wheeze or crackles may be heard, and pursed‑lip breathing is common in COPD.
